LESSON MENU
CONTROL INSTRUCTIONS

Control instructions are used in PLCs to change the location where instructions are being evaluated. This can be within the same ladder, or in a different ladder, depending on the instruction you use....
DISCUSSION
Before we look at the different control instructions available, let's discuss the pros and cons of using these types of instructions.

Often, you may want to repeat a small section of ladder logic in sections of your program. For example, after every step in a process, you might want a light to flash and an output to be sent to a terminal attached to the PLC...
Let's say there are 14 steps to your process, with 10 rungs of ladder logic required to turn on the light and send information to the terminal attached to the PLC.

If you entered all of these rungs, over and over again, at the points they were needed, you would have 140 rungs in your code. Instead of typing these repeatedly, we add another ladder to our program...

This new ladder requires a special control instruction at the beginning and end which makes our 10 lines now 12. Also, at each point where the code is needed, one rung is added to the main ladder logic code. This results in an additional 14 rungs.....

The final total is only 26 rungs instead of 140. You can see that using this type of feature, normally referred to as a subroutine, is very beneficial in large programs, particularly in systems with memory constraints...

There are two important problem situations to avoid when using subroutines. The first is calling too many subroutines within subroutines; the second is not returning to the main ladder logic for output and input refreshing...reshing.

Most PLCs allow subroutines within subroutines. However, there is normally a limit to the number of levels. For the PLC you are using, you can go 4 levels deep. In other words, the main ladder can call a subroutine that calls a subroutine that calls a subroutine that calls a subroutine...

To avoid the second problem situation, make sure the program eventually returns to the main ladder in order to update inputs and outputs on time. This problem occurs more with jumping than subroutines........
Jumping is the control ability to move to a different part of any ladder including the ladder that contains the instruction. Jumping requires a label at the location that you want to jump to.
Now that you have a basic understanding of the important concepts of control instructions, let's examine the control instructions of the PLC in detail.
The six instructions we will examine are listed in the table below. The instructions have been grouped into the sets that are used together to provide a control function.
This is the Jump to Label (JMP) instruction. It is used to change the current rung execution to a label numbered the same as the number you specify.

For this instruction to work, the label must exist and have the same number you entered in the instruction. The range of number values is 0 to 999. Remember, when jumping, don't get stuck in an endless loop...
If you are stuck in an endless loop that doesn't allow the ladder logic program to cycle, the inputs and outputs will not be updated. This will cause your program to run incorrectly.
This instruction is the Label (LBL) instruction. It is used with the Jump to Label instruction to allow a change in the point where instruction evaluation is taking place.
This instruction requires a label number between 0 and 999 that corresponds to the same label number specified by the Jump to Label instruction. Again, be careful for infinite or endless loops.

This instruction is the Jump to Subroutine (JSR) instruction. It is used to move code evaluation to another file in memory known as a subroutine. This is another file that contains a different ladder logic program with subroutine instructions.s.
The only parameter this instruction needs is the number of the file that you want to jump to. This value is between 3 and 255 and represents a ladder logic program you have entered.
This instruction is the Subroutine (SBR) instruction. It requires no parameters and should be in the first rung of all subroutines.
No information is needed because the Jump to Subroutine instruction knows from the file number where the subroutine resides.

This instruction is the Return from Subroutine (RET) instruction. It is contained within a subroutine at the point where the subroutine has finished and evaluation should return to the main ladder logic program or another subroutine...

When this instruction is evaluated, the PLC begins evaluating code immediately following the Jump to Subroutine instruction that called this subroutine. The RET instruction has no required parameters...
Which instruction is used to jump to a subroutine?
Remember, the (J)ump to (S)ub(R)outine instruction is used to leave the main program and run a separate routine before returning to the main program.
TRY AGAIN!
The last instruction that we will look at is conceptually different than the other control instructions.
This is the Master Control Reset (MCR) instruction. It requires no parameters and is used to enable or disable a section of rungs.
If there are rungs in your ladder that should only be evaluated at specific times, this is the instruction you would use.
Prior to the code you wish to control, the MCR instruction is inserted. The logic path before the instruction controls whether the ladder logic is evaluated after this point.
At the end of the ladder logic code you want disabled, you add another MCR instruction by itself on a rung. You cannot put anything before the second MCR instruction.

If you had an XIC instruction before the first MCR instruction, and that XIC instruction was looking at a push button switch attached to the inputs, the code after this point would only be evaluated if the button were pushed in...
The only thing you cannot do is assign a Jump to Label instruction to an MCR section. You wouldn't know if this section were enabled or disabled, and errors could result.
How many MCR instructions are used together to provide a control operation?
The Master Control Reset operation requires the use of two MCR instructions to enable and disable a section of code.
TRY AGAIN!
As you can see, the control instructions provide a method for optimizing ladder logic programs for speed and performance.
As your familiarization with these instructions grows, you will tend use to them more and more to make your code smaller and modular. Modular means in smaller manageable pieces.
This completes the information on CONTROL INSTRUCTIONS.....
1. The Jump to Label (JMP) instruction is used to move code evaluation from the current point to a point in the ladder logic where there is a corresponding label.

2. The Label (LBL) instruction gives the location to which the Jump to Label instruction should move the code evaluation.LBL) instruction gives the location to which the Jump to Label instruction should move the code evaluation.....................
3. The Jump to Subroutine (JSR) instruction is used to change the location of code evaluation to another ladder logic file.
4. The Subroutine (SBR) instruction is used at the beginning of a file to indicate that the file is a subroutine.

5. The Return from Subroutine (RET) instruction is used in a subroutine to indicate that you want to return to the location where the subroutine evaluation was started. Code evaluation begins after the JSR instruction that called the subroutine.
6. The Master Control Reset (MCR) instruction is used in pairs to enable or disable sections of code based on the logic path preceding the first MCR instruction.

Before entering the program into the PLC APS software, let's look at what the program should do. This will help us understand if the program is operating properly when we test it.

The first program is the main ladder logic program. The first rung enables output LED 0 every time this rung is evaluated. The second rung contains an instruction to examine the slide switch input and the Master Control Reset instruction...

If the switch is in the right (ON) position, the logic path to the MCR instruction is false. This causes all codes between this MCR instruction and the next MCR instruction to be ignored. If the switch is in the left (OFF) position, the code will be evaluated.

The next rung sets the LED 1 output to true when this rung is evaluated. This rung is only evaluated when the MCR instruction in the preceding logic path is true. This allows us to know if we are evaluating code inside the MCR block...
The next instruction is the closing MCR instruction. Remember, MCR instructions are used in pairs, and the second MCR instruction has no instructions preceding it in the rung.

The last instruction of the main ladder jumps to the subroutine stored in file 4. When that subroutine finishes, it returns to the point just after the Jump to Subroutine instruction. This will be the point where the main cycle ends in this program...

The subroutine contains two rungs. The first rung contains the SBR subroutine instruction which just indicates that this is a subroutine. The second instruction in the first rung sets output LED 2 true. This allows us to know when the subroutine is being used...

The last instruction of the subroutine contains the Return from Subroutine (RET) instruction. As mentioned earlier, the RET instruction brings evaluation back to the ladder program that called the subroutine. Code evaluation resumes just after the instruction that called the subroutine...
As you can see, the LEDs will indicate which rungs of the ladder logic are being executed. Look at the code and try to predict what the output of this program will be.
